title: Alley bar and butchers at the market
summary: Frazier and the interviewer talk about how meat was sold and kept before refrigerators, and how simple life was.

blocks.x: Right in the alley, you see they had a bar in like a little nightclub, you could call it, right in the back. Like the bar, you come into the alley between the market and the Steinmetz and Ocean's store, and as you come in through that alley like that, you come into, it'd be like a regular bar, you know? I see, yeah. Of course, that would control the people off now by having that seminar circles, and the circle people, they come in there later years after. But I'm bringing it back to a time when you had, the meat wouldn't be in these refrigerators like these people, they'd be on the butcher stands, they'd come there early in the morning, and they'd hang up upon like on these hooks. The stand view, you know, open stands, you see? Yeah. And you could then, when the market closed between 12-1 and the daytime, where they'd put their meats in these big old, old-time ice boxes on the outside. Oh, I see. So, yeah. And the Iceman, you had no fridges there, the Iceman used to pack the, you know, the packed ice on the meat. And every early Sunday mornings like that, where the markets would be open, you know, you could see that all over the door. The first year had wagons, horse drawings with two horses or two mules, bringing the meat from the Christian City Slaughter Company, or either the Northern Butcher Abattoir, bringing the meat to these different butcher stands, and then they'd turn around and put it on the stand, it's like that, even before the bitches, you know, get there. And when the butchers come, maybe 5 o'clock in the morning, well, they start cutting meat like they want to hang it up on them hooks. And then, of course, during them times, you had no border help to say that the meat could just be spoiled, you understand? And that's how the meat was sold. And then mostly, then you had the live chickens, chickens being cages. You could buy a live chicken, they could, you know, kill it right there for you, or you would take it home yourself, you know, and bring it in your market basket.
That's what, yeah, everybody would come every morning and do their shopping.

That's right. Yeah, do their shopping. They liked the day people could buy so much meat and all, half a side of a beef, or a cow like that, and stir it away. Freeze it all over there. Freeze it all over there for months and months, you know. That's like, people.
Sounds like a, it sounds like a very, you know, pleasant way to live, very uncomplicated.

Yeah, it was, people lived healthy. I mean, during the days, we didn't have freezer days, but they sure bought the meat like that, and they had it live on, you know, on the meat stands. And then, it used to do you good to see the, when they closed during the daytime, they used to take like these, these long, we call them cane knives, you know, and scrape, you know, like the meat stains off the, off the, off the meat stand, you see. They used to scrape that down.
